avodah_zarah-2b-1-15.note: In the future, God holds up a Torah scroll and invites whoever studied it to take a reward. Rome enters first and says it built markets and bathhouses and amassed silver and gold, all so the Jewish people could study Torah. God calls them fools: the markets were for prostitutes, the bathhouses for their own pleasure, and the silver and gold are His. They leave disappointed. Persia comes next, claiming its bridges, conquered cities and wars were for Israel; God answers that the bridges were for tolls, the cities for forced labor, and the wars were His. Every nation tries in turn. They then plead that they would have accepted the Torah had God held a mountain over them as He did over Israel. God answers: you accepted seven commandments, so where did you keep them?
avodah_zarah-2b-1-15.why: The Gemara is expounding a verse from Isaiah about the nations gathering for judgment: "Who among them can declare this?" This scene acts out the verse line by line, with "this" read as the Torah.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who judges the nations and answers each of their claims.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage quoted that God offered the Torah to every nation, and none accepted it but Israel.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage quoted that when a king and a community are judged, the king goes first.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage quoted that the bear in Daniel's vision is Persia.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Hama
people.about: A Sage quoted that God held Mount Sinai over Israel like a basin.

terms.meaning: Seven basic commandments, such as not to murder or steal, that the Sages taught apply to all humanity, the descendants of Noah.
Forced labor that a ruler could demand of the people of a conquered place.

terms.term: overturned the mountain like a basin
terms.meaning: A teaching that at Sinai God held the mountain over Israel like an upturned tub and told them to accept the Torah or be buried there.

avodah_zarah-4a-10-13.note: Rabbi Abbahu praised Rav Safra to the heretics as a great man, and because of that they let him off his taxes for thirteen years. One day they met Rav Safra and asked him about a verse in Amos: if God loves Israel, why does He punish them for all their sins? Does one who is angry take it out on the one he loves? Rav Safra was silent. They threw a scarf around his neck and tormented him. Rabbi Abbahu came upon them and explained that he had praised Rav Safra's learning in the Oral Law, not in the Bible; Sages in the Land of Israel study verses closely because they must debate the heretics. When they asked him for the answer, he gave a parable: a man who lends to a friend and to an enemy collects from the friend little by little, and from the enemy all at once.
avodah_zarah-4a-10-13.why: The Gemara has been explaining that God punishes Israel for each sin in small portions so as not to destroy them all at once, and that their sufferings in this world are meant for their good. Rabbi Abbahu's parable makes the same point.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage who praised Rav Safra to the heretics, then rescued him and answered their question.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage whose tax was remitted on Rabbi Abbahu's word, and who could not answer the heretics about the verse.

terms.meaning: The English translation's word for people who argued with the Sages about the meaning of Scripture.
The early Sages whose teachings make up the Mishna and related works. Rabbi Abbahu means Rav Safra is an expert in their oral teachings.
A short illustrative tale, often about a king or an ordinary person, used to explain a teaching.

avodah_zarah-4b-7-8.note: A heretic kept tormenting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with challenges about verses. One day Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi took a rooster, set it between the legs of his bed and watched it, planning to curse the heretic at the exact moment when God is angry. When that moment came, he fell asleep. He concluded that it is not proper to do such a thing, since Scripture says God's mercies are over all His works and that punishing even the righteous is not good.
avodah_zarah-4b-7-8.why: Abaye has just taught that God is angry for a moment within the first three hours of the day, and that the sign is a rooster's comb turning fully white. The story shows a Sage trying to use that sign.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: A Sage harassed by a heretic, who tried to curse him at the moment of God's anger.

terms.meaning: The English translation's word for someone who argued with the Sages about the meaning of Scripture.
The Gemara teaches that God's anger lasts only an instant each day; a curse spoken then was thought to take effect.

avodah_zarah-6b-5-5.note: A heretic sent a Caesarean dinar, a Roman coin, to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia on the day of his festival. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia asked Reish Lakish, who was sitting before him, what to do: if he took it, the man would go and give thanks to his idol; if he refused, the man would bear him a grudge. Reish Lakish said to take it and throw it into a pit in front of him. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia objected that this would make the grudge even worse. Reish Lakish explained that he meant to do it in an offhand way, as if it slipped from his hand.
avodah_zarah-6b-5-5.why: The Mishna forbids doing business with idol worshippers around their festivals, and the Gemara explains that the worry is the gentile will thank his idol for his success. This gift on the festival day is a case of that worry in real life.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: A Sage who received the coin and asked what to do with it.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage sitting before Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, who told him how to get rid of it.

terms.meaning: The English translation's word here for a non-Jew who worshipped idols and kept their festivals.
A Roman coin, probably one minted with the emperor's image.

avodah_zarah-8b-4-7.note: Rav Dimi reported that the Romans fought thirty-two battles against the Greeks and could not beat them until they made an alliance with the Jewish people. Their terms: if the kings come from us, the governors come from you, and the reverse. The Romans then sent the Greeks a riddle to settle the matter by judgment. Which should be set beneath which: a pearl or a precious stone? The Greeks answered that the pearl goes under the precious stone, the precious stone under the onyx, and the onyx under the Torah scroll. The Romans replied: then we have the Torah scroll, and Israel is with us. They forced the Greeks to submit. For twenty-six years the Romans kept faith with the Jewish people, and after that they subjugated them.
avodah_zarah-8b-4-7.why: The Mishna lists Kratesis among Roman festivals, and Rav Yosef says Rome seized an empire twice, once in the days of the Greeks. Rav Dimi's account explains that earlier conquest.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel and reported this account.

terms.meaning: A Roman festival listed in the Mishna, which the Gemara links to the day Rome seized control of an empire.
Governors: officials who ruled provinces under the king.
The translation's word here for an especially valuable precious stone.

avodah_zarah-8b-12-14.note: The wicked kingdom of Rome decreed that anyone who ordained judges would be killed, anyone ordained would be killed, the city where it happened would be destroyed, and its surrounding area uprooted. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava went and sat between two large mountains and two large cities, between Usha and Shefaram, and ordained five Elders there: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua; Rav Avya adds Rabbi Nehemya. When enemies found them, he told them, "My sons, run!" They asked what would become of him. He said he was lying before them like a stone that cannot be turned over. It was said that the soldiers did not leave until they had driven three hundred iron spears into his body and made it like a sieve.
avodah_zarah-8b-12-14.why: Rav says that without Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava the laws of fines would have been lost, and the Gemara asks how, since one could just study them. It answers that only ordained judges can rule on fines, and this story shows how he kept ordination alive against Rome's decree.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: A Sage who ordained new judges in defiance of the Roman decree and was killed for it.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: One of the five Elders he ordained.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua
people.about: One of the five Elders he ordained.

people.name: Rav Avya
people.about: A Sage who adds that Rabbi Nehemya was also ordained.

terms.meaning: The formal appointment of a Sage as a judge, passed from teacher to student. Only ordained judges could rule in certain cases, such as fines.
Penalties set by the Torah at a fixed amount, beyond simple repayment for damage. Only ordained judges could impose them.
The limit around a town beyond which one may not walk on the Sabbath. Sitting between two of them meant being in no town's area.

avodah_zarah-10a-13-14.note: The Roman emperor Antoninus told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi he wanted two things: for his son Asveirus to rule after him, and for Tiberias to be freed from taxes. The Roman leaders would grant one request but not two. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi set one man on another's shoulders, gave a dove to the one on top, and told the one below to tell him to let it fly. Antoninus understood: ask for his son to rule, and have his son free Tiberias. When Antoninus complained that important Romans were troubling him, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi took him to his garden and each day pulled up one radish in front of him. Antoninus understood: kill them one by one, and do not provoke them all at once.
avodah_zarah-10a-13-14.why: The Gemara has said that the Romans do sometimes make a king's son king at the king's request, giving Asveirus son of Antoninus as the example. This story shows how that came about. Afterward the Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not simply speak openly.

people.name: Antoninus
people.about: A Roman emperor who seeks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's advice.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; answers Antoninus with silent demonstrations.

people.name: Asveirus
people.about: Antoninus' son, whom he wants to succeed him.

terms.meaning: A city in the Land of Israel.
Antoninus wants Tiberias exempted from paying taxes to Rome.

avodah_zarah-10b-1-1.note: The Roman emperor Antoninus, a friend of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, had a daughter named Gira who had sexual relations outside marriage. Too discreet to say so openly, the two talked in plants whose names made puns. Antoninus sent a rocket plant, hinting that she had strayed; Rabbi sent coriander, hinting that she deserved death; Antoninus sent leeks, meaning he would be cut off if he did that; and Rabbi sent back lettuce, meaning: have mercy on her.
avodah_zarah-10b-1-1.why: It is one of a run of stories about the secret friendship of Antoninus and Rabbi, told just after the Gemara explains why Rabbi always answered the emperor in coded gestures: he feared that powerful Romans would overhear him.

people.name: Antoninus
people.about: A Roman emperor who, in Talmudic tradition, was a close and secret friend of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Leader of the Jews of the Land of Israel around 200 CE and editor of the Mishna; often called simply Rabbi.

people.name: Gira
people.about: Antoninus's daughter, whose conduct prompts the exchange.

avodah_zarah-10b-3-5.note: Antoninus had a tunnel running from his house to the house of Rabbi. Each day he brought two servants, killed one at Rabbi's door and the other at his own, so no one would know of his visits. He told Rabbi to let no one be with him when he came. One day he found Rabbi Hanina bar Hama sitting there. Rabbi said this was no ordinary human being. Antoninus told Rabbi Hanina to go and wake the servant sleeping at the entrance. Rabbi Hanina found the servant had been killed. Not wanting to bring bad news, nor to slight the king by ignoring him, he prayed for mercy, revived the servant and sent him in. Antoninus said: I know even the least of you can revive the dead, but still let no one be with you when I come.
avodah_zarah-10b-3-5.why: This is one of a run of stories about the secret friendship between Antoninus and Rabbi, which the Gemara tells after explaining how Antoninus's son came to rule.

people.name: Antoninus
people.about: A Roman ruler who visited Rabbi in secret.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the leading Sage, Antoninus's friend.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Hama
people.about: A Sage found with Rabbi, who revived the dead servant through prayer.

avodah_zarah-10b-10-14.note: A Roman emperor who hated the Jews asked his nobles whether a man with a sore on his foot should cut it off and live, or leave it and suffer. They said cut it off. Ketia son of Shalom objected: the Jews can never all be destroyed, and Rome would be called the severed kingdom. The emperor agreed but said whoever defeats the king in argument is thrown into a furnace. As Ketia was led away, a noblewoman said: woe to the ship that sails without paying its tax. He circumcised himself and said he had paid his tax. As he was thrown in, he left all his property to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues. A Divine Voice declared Ketia destined for the World-to-Come, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi wept: some earn their world in one moment, others over many years.
avodah_zarah-10b-10-14.why: A teaching reads the verse placing Edom's leaders in the netherworld as not including all its officers; the exception is Ketia son of Shalom. The Gemara asks who he was, and this story answers.

people.name: Ketia son of Shalom
people.about: A Roman official who argues against destroying the Jews and is put to death.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Receives Ketia's property with his colleagues and teaches how to divide it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; weeps when he hears the Divine Voice.

terms.meaning: Here a figure of speech for the Jewish people, whom the emperor wanted to remove.
A place of execution where a person was thrown to die.
A voice from Heaven announcing God's view.
The life after death promised to the righteous.

avodah_zarah-11a-1-4.note: Onkelos bar Kelonimos, a Roman, converted to Judaism, and the emperor sent a troop of soldiers to seize him. Onkelos drew them in with verses, and they converted. A second troop, told not to say anything to him, heard him point out that every official holds a torch before a greater one, yet God held a torch before the Jewish people in the wilderness; they converted too. A third troop, told not to converse with him at all, saw him put his hand on a mezuza and explain that God guards His servants from outside their homes. They also converted, and after that the emperor sent no more soldiers after him.
avodah_zarah-11a-1-4.why: The Gemara has been telling of Romans drawn to Judaism, such as Ketia and Antoninus, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's companion; this account of Onkelos continues that thread before the discussion returns to Antoninus.

people.name: Onkelos bar Kelonimos
people.about: A Roman who converted to Judaism and won over the soldiers sent to arrest him.

people.name: The emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who sent three troops of soldiers to bring Onkelos back.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll with verses from the Torah, fixed to the doorpost of a Jewish home.

terms.term: the Holy One, Blessed be He
terms.meaning: A common rabbinic way of referring to God.

avodah_zarah-11b-2-3.note: Shmuel describes a festival held in Rome once every seventy years. A healthy man is made to ride on a lame man, dressed in the garments of Adam, the first man, with the scalp of the executed sage Rabbi Yishmael on his head and gold hung on his neck, while the markets are covered with onyx. Heralds announce before him that Jacob's calculation of the redemption is fraudulent and that Esau is a forger, and they end: Woe to this one, Esau, when that one, Jacob, will arise.
avodah_zarah-11b-2-3.why: The mishna lists the festivals of the gentiles, and the Gemara adds this Roman one; right after, it explains that the mishna leaves it out because it lists only festivals held every year.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who describes the festival, as reported by his student Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage whose scalp, flayed by the Romans when they executed him, is placed on the rider's head.

terms.meaning: The twin sons of Isaac and Rebecca. The Sages read Esau as a symbol of Rome and Jacob as a symbol of the Jewish people; Jacob limped after wrestling with an angel.

avodah_zarah-13a-11-11.note: Rabbi Yosei recalls an incident: Yosef the priest followed his teacher to the city of Sidon, outside the Land of Israel, in order to learn Torah. Rabbi Yohanan rules that the law follows Rabbi Yosei.
avodah_zarah-13a-11-11.why: A baraita asks whether a priest may leave the Land of Israel, and so become ritually impure, to study Torah when teachers are available at home. Rabbi Yosei says he may, since one does not learn from everyone, and cites Yosef the priest as precedent.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who tells of the incident to support his ruling.

people.name: Yosef the priest
people.about: A priest who left the Land of Israel to follow his teacher to Sidon to learn Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who rules that the law follows Rabbi Yosei.

terms.meaning: A descendant of Aaron (a kohen). Priests must avoid certain kinds of ritual impurity, and the Sages treated lands outside Israel as impure.
Jewish law; the binding ruling.

avodah_zarah-16a-9-9.note: Shmuel reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household had to present the authorities with a fattened ox on their festival day. They paid forty thousand dinars so they could bring it the day after the festival instead, another forty thousand so they could bring it slaughtered rather than alive, and another forty thousand so they would not have to bring it at all.
avodah_zarah-16a-9-9.why: The Gemara asks whether one may sell a gentile a fattened ox, which might later be kept for work, and tries this case as proof. It rejects the proof: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi simply wanted to end the practice step by step.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The head of the household that paid to escape the gift of an ox; called simply Rabbi in the text.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident, through Rav Yehuda.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; forty thousand dinars was a very large sum.
An ox fed up for slaughter rather than kept for plowing or other work.

avodah_zarah-16b-14-16.note: Rabbi Eliezer was arrested on a charge of heresy and brought before a tribunal. When the officer asked why an elder like him would engage in such frivolous matters, he answered that he trusted the Judge, meaning God; the officer thought he meant him and acquitted him. At home Rabbi Eliezer refused his students' consolation, until Rabbi Akiva suggested he had once enjoyed some heretical teaching. Rabbi Eliezer remembered meeting Ya'akov of Kefar Sekhanya, a student of Jesus the Nazarene, in the market of Tzippori, who taught him an interpretation of a verse in Jesus' name that pleased him. He concluded that this was why he had been arrested, since he had come too close to heresy.
avodah_zarah-16b-14-16.why: The mishna forbids helping gentiles build a tribunal, a place where people are sentenced to death; this leads the Gemara to tell of Sages who were brought before the Roman authorities for judgment.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage arrested for heresy and acquitted, who later traced his arrest to a heretic's teaching he had enjoyed.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's student, who helps him see why he was arrested.

people.name: Ya'akov of Kefar Sekhanya
people.about: A student of Jesus the Nazarene whom Rabbi Eliezer met in the market of Tzippori.

people.name: Jesus the Nazarene
people.about: The teacher in whose name Ya'akov passed on the interpretation.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who rules that one must keep four cubits from a prostitute.

terms.meaning: Here, the teachings of sectarian groups the Sages considered outside Judaism, including early followers of Jesus.
The Torah forbids bringing a prostitute's fee as an offering to the Temple; Ya'akov asked whether it could pay for a bathroom for the High Priest.
An ancient measure of length, roughly half a meter; four cubits is about two meters.

avodah_zarah-17a-8-10.note: A woman came to Rav Hisda to confess. She said the lightest of her sins was that she had conceived her younger son with her older son. Rav Hisda said to prepare her burial shrouds, but she did not die.
avodah_zarah-17a-8-10.why: The Gemara has read a verse in Proverbs as saying that people who turn back from heresy die. It asks whether that is always so, and brings this woman, whose worst sins implied heresy, as a case where it did not happen; she had not truly repented, it answers.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage to whom the woman confesses.

terms.meaning: The cloth garments a dead body is wrapped in; Rav Hisda is saying she will soon die.
Here, turning away from Jewish belief; the Gemara infers she had done this as well.

avodah_zarah-17a-11-15.note: Elazar ben Durdayya had been with every prostitute in the world. Hearing of one overseas who charged a purse of dinars, he took the money and crossed seven rivers to reach her; during the act she passed wind and said that, like the wind, he would never be accepted in repentance. Shaken, he sat between mountains and begged the mountains and hills, heaven and earth, sun and moon, and stars and constellations to pray for mercy for him, and each said it must pray for itself. Concluding that it depended only on him, he put his head between his knees and cried until his soul left him. A Divine Voice declared him destined for the World-to-Come, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi wept that some acquire their world in one moment, adding that penitents are even called Rabbi.
avodah_zarah-17a-11-15.why: The Gemara has claimed that a heretic who repents dies soon after, and asks whether that is true of sexual sin too. Elazar ben Durdayya died on repenting; the Gemara answers that his attachment to sin was so strong it resembled heresy.

people.name: Elazar ben Durdayya
people.about: A man notorious for visiting prostitutes, who repented and died weeping.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; he wept on hearing the story and said penitents are even called Rabbi.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of rabbinic law.
A voice from Heaven announcing God's decision, a common device in rabbinic stories.
The life of reward after this world.

avodah_zarah-17a-16-16.note: Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yonatan were walking and came to a fork: one path led past a place of idol worship, the other past a brothel. One proposed the idol path, since the urge for idol worship had been slaughtered; the other proposed the brothel path, so they could overcome their urge and be rewarded. When they got there, the prostitutes withdrew before them. Asked how he had known this would happen, the second cited the verse that discernment will guard you from lewdness.
avodah_zarah-17a-16-16.why: The Gemara has been teaching that one must keep far from heresy and from prostitutes; this story of two Sages choosing their path between idol worship and a brothel follows on that theme.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage walking with Rabbi Yonatan; the text does not say which of the two proposed which path.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan
people.about: A Sage walking with Rabbi Hanina.

terms.meaning: The inner urge to sin. The Sages taught that the urge to worship idols had been slaughtered, that is, removed from the world.

avodah_zarah-17b-3-13.note: The Romans arrested Rabbi Elazar ben Perata on five charges and Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon on one. Hanina told Elazar he would be saved, because he had done acts of kindness as well as study Torah, while Hanina would not. At his trial Elazar denied teaching Torah and stealing, and miracles backed him: hornets showed which wool was warp and which woof, and an old man was trampled at the house of Abidan that day, as he said he feared. When a man rose to testify that he had freed his slave, Elijah flung a letter the man carried four hundred parasangs, and the man went after it and never came back. Hanina, asked why he taught Torah, said 'As the Lord my God commanded me.' He was sentenced to burning, his wife to execution, his daughter to a brothel.
avodah_zarah-17b-3-13.why: The Gemara returns to the Sages tried by the Romans. Along the way it uses Hanina's words to teach, with Rav Huna, that Torah study without acts of kindness is not enough, and it explains what each of the three had done to deserve their sentence.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Perata
people.about: A Sage arrested by the Romans on five charges, who is saved through a series of miracles.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon
people.about: A Sage arrested for teaching Torah in public, sentenced to burning; the Gemara says he pronounced God's name in public.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who appears disguised as a Roman nobleman to stop a witness against Rabbi Elazar ben Perata.

terms.meaning: The two sets of threads in weaving: the warp is stretched on the loom and the woof is passed through it. An expert weaver can tell them apart.
A meeting place where debates on wisdom and faith were held, which the Romans expected Rabbi Elazar ben Perata to attend.
God's proper name, which by tradition is not pronounced as it is written.
A Persian measure of distance, roughly four kilometers; four hundred of them is a very great distance.

avodah_zarah-18a-4-4.note: As Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon, his wife and his daughter went out after being sentenced, each of them accepted God's judgment as just with a verse. He said, "The Rock, His work is perfect"; his wife continued, "A God of faithfulness and without iniquity"; and his daughter said, "Great in counsel, and mighty in work." Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: How great these righteous people are, that three verses of accepting judgment came to them at the moment they accepted it.
avodah_zarah-18a-4-4.why: The Gemara has just explained why Heaven decreed each of the three sentences, his for saying God's name in public, his wife's for not protesting, his daughter's for her vanity; now it shows all three accepting the verdict as just.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon
people.about: A Sage sentenced by the Romans to death by burning.

people.name: His wife
people.about: Sentenced to execution; she completes her husband's verse.

people.name: His daughter
people.about: Sentenced to sit in a brothel; she adds a verse from Jeremiah.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; he praises the three for their verses.

terms.meaning: Declaring that God's decree is just even when it brings suffering; still part of Jewish mourning practice.

avodah_zarah-18a-5-12.note: When Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma fell ill, Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon visited him and was warned that Rome would burn him and his Torah scroll for teaching in public. Asked if he had a place in the World-to-Come, Hanina told how he gave his own Purim money to the poor, and Yosei wished to share his lot. Days later Yosei died, and Roman notables returning from his funeral found Hanina teaching in public. They wrapped him in his scroll and burned him, with wet wool on his heart to slow his death. He saw the letters flying upward and would not open his mouth to the fire. The executioner raised the flame and removed the wool for a promise of the World-to-Come, then leaped into the fire; a Divine Voice declared both destined for it, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi wept.
avodah_zarah-18a-5-12.why: The Gemara has been following Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon's arrest and sentence by the Romans, and here tells how the sentence of burning was carried out.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma
people.about: A Sage, called teacher by Hanina, who warned him that Rome would burn him.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon
people.about: A Sage who kept teaching Torah in public and was burned alive by the Romans.

people.name: His daughter
people.about: Watches her father's burning and asks how she can see him like this.

people.name: The executioner
people.about: The Roman who hastened Hanina's death and then threw himself into the fire.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; he wept on hearing what the Divine Voice declared.

terms.meaning: Money set aside for the festival of Purim. Hanina mixed his up with charity funds and gave all of it to the poor.
A voice from Heaven announcing God's decision.
The life of reward after this world.

avodah_zarah-18a-13-15.note: Berurya, Rabbi Meir's wife, could not bear that her sister was sitting in a brothel, so Rabbi Meir took a vessel of dinars and went, reasoning that a miracle would happen only if she had not sinned. Disguised as a knight, he propositioned her; she put him off, and he concluded she had done no wrong. He gave her guard the money and taught him to say "God of Meir answer me!", proving it by escaping man-eating dogs, and the guard handed her over. Later the guard was taken to be hanged, said the words and was let down, and told the whole story; the Romans engraved Rabbi Meir's face at the gate of Rome. Chased one day, he ducked into a brothel and escaped, either by pretending to eat gentile food or because Elijah, disguised as a prostitute, embraced him; then he fled to Babylonia.
avodah_zarah-18a-13-15.why: The Gemara has just told that the Romans sentenced Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon's daughter to sit in a brothel, and explained why Heaven allowed it; this tells how her sister's husband rescued her.

people.name: Berurya
people.about: Rabbi Meir's wife, a daughter of Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon, who asks him to save her sister.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who rescues his wife's sister from a Roman brothel and becomes a hunted man.

people.name: The guard
people.about: The man guarding the sister, who takes the bribe and is later saved from hanging.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who in one version appears as a prostitute to save Rabbi Meir from capture.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; a vessel full of them was a large fortune.
The Sages forbade Jews to eat it, so the Romans would not believe that a man eating it could be Rabbi Meir.

avodah_zarah-19a-5-5.note: Levi and Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, were studying before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. When they finished a book, Levi asked for Proverbs and Rabbi Shimon for Psalms; Rabbi Shimon overruled Levi, and Psalms was brought. When they reached the verse "But his delight is in the Torah of the Lord", Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi explained that a person can learn Torah only from the part his heart desires. Levi said: My teacher, you have just given me permission to get up and leave.
avodah_zarah-19a-5-5.why: The Gemara has quoted Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's teaching that one learns only what his heart desires; this incident shows the occasion on which he said it, and how his student turned it back on him.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A student of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi who wanted to study Proverbs.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who insisted on studying Psalms.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi in the text; the teacher of both, and Rabbi Shimon's father.

avodah_zarah-19a-18-18.note: Rav Hisda told the Sages studying with him that he wanted to tell them something but was afraid that they would then leave him: that anyone who learns Torah from one teacher never sees a sign of blessing. They did leave him and went to learn from Rava. Rav Hisda then told them that this applies only to reasoning; for learning the tradition itself it is better to have one teacher, so as not to be confused by different versions.
avodah_zarah-19a-18-18.why: The school of Rabbi Yannai has just read the verse comparing a scholar to a replanted tree to mean that one should learn from many teachers; Rav Hisda's students act on exactly that teaching, and he limits it.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who feared his students would leave him, and did lose them to Rava.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage to whom Rav Hisda's students went.

people.name: Rabbi Tanhum bar Hanilai
people.about: A Sage who teaches that one should divide one's study into Bible, Mishna and Talmud.

terms.meaning: The memorized oral teachings themselves, as opposed to the reasoning used to analyze them.

avodah_zarah-19b-8-8.note: Rabbi Alexandri would call out in public like a merchant selling his wares: Who wants life? Who wants life? Everyone crowded around him, saying: Give us life! He answered them with the verse "Who is the man that desires life... Keep your tongue from evil."
avodah_zarah-19b-8-8.why: The Gemara is collecting teachings that Torah study brings success; right after this verse it explains that the psalm's next words, "do good", mean studying Torah, not only avoiding evil speech.

people.name: Rabbi Alexandri
people.about: A Sage who called out in the street offering life to anyone who wanted it.

avodah_zarah-20a-9-9.note: Two incidents are told. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, standing on a step on the Temple Mount, saw an exceptionally beautiful gentile woman and said, "How great are Your works, O Lord!" Rabbi Akiva saw the wife of the wicked Turnus Rufus and spat, laughed and cried: he spat because she came from a putrid drop, laughed because she was destined to convert and he would marry her, and cried because such beauty would end up consumed by dirt.
avodah_zarah-20a-9-9.why: Rav has ruled that one may not say how beautiful a gentile woman is. The Gemara raises these incidents as an objection, and answers that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was thanking God for His creatures, not praising the woman.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: A Sage who praised God on seeing a beautiful gentile woman.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who spat, laughed and cried on seeing the wife of Turnus Rufus.

people.name: Turnus Rufus
people.about: Called wicked in the text; his wife was destined to convert and marry Rabbi Akiva.

terms.meaning: The hill in Jerusalem on which the Temple stood.
A blunt rabbinic phrase for the seed from which every person is conceived, a reminder of human lowliness.

avodah_zarah-20b-2-2.note: This is a short answer, not a full story. The Gemara explains that Rabban Gamliel did not look at the beautiful woman on purpose: he was walking around a corner, and they came upon each other unexpectedly as each of them turned.
avodah_zarah-20b-2-2.why: A baraita has just taught that a man may not gaze at a beautiful woman; this answers how the Sage in the earlier incident, who saw a beautiful gentile woman on the Temple Mount and praised God, could have looked at her.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who saw the beautiful woman; the translation explains he met her by chance at a corner.

avodah_zarah-22a-2-4.note: Some saffron growers, a gentile and a Jew, shared a field: the gentile worked it on Shabbat and the Jew on Sunday. They came before Rava, who permitted the arrangement. Ravina challenged him with a baraita that allows such a split only if it was agreed at the outset, and Rava was embarrassed; in the end it came out that the partners had agreed on it from the start.
avodah_zarah-22a-2-4.why: The Gemara has been discussing when a Jew may let a gentile or Samaritan work his field on days when Jews may not work. Right after, it gives another version of the case, and then says Ravina meant to support Rava and the embarrassment never happened.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who permitted the partnership.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who challenged Rava's ruling from a baraita.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest on which Jews may not work and may not profit from work done for them.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of rabbinic law.

avodah_zarah-22b-11-11.note: Two Sages report what they saw. Rabbi Hanina, as Shmuel quotes him, saw a gentile buy a goose in the market, have sex with it, strangle it, roast it and eat it. Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti saw an Arab buy a thigh of meat in the market, carve a hole in it for penetration, penetrate it, roast it and eat it.
avodah_zarah-22b-11-11.why: The discussion has been about why a Jew may not leave his animals alone with gentiles, whom it suspects of bestiality. It now asks whether the same holds for birds, and these reports are its proof that it does.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who reports seeing a gentile abuse a goose; quoted by Shmuel through Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
people.about: A Sage who reports what he saw an Arab do with a thigh of meat.

terms.meaning: Sexual relations with an animal, which the Torah forbids.

avodah_zarah-23b-10-10.note: The Sages asked Rabbi Eliezer how far one must go to honor one's parents. He told them of Dama ben Netina, a gentile in Ashkelon. The Sages once wanted to buy precious stones from him for the High Priest's ephod at a profit of six hundred thousand gold dinars (Rav Kahana says eight hundred thousand), but the keys to the chest lay under his sleeping father's head, and he would not disturb him. The next year a red heifer was born in his herd. When the Sages came to buy it, he told them he knew they would pay anything he asked, but he wanted only the money he had lost by not waking his father.
avodah_zarah-23b-10-10.why: Rabbi Eliezer forbids buying a red heifer from gentiles, and Sheila reads that from the words 'that they take'. The Gemara uses this story to object: the same words appear for the Tabernacle gifts, yet the Sages tried to buy ephod stones, and even a heifer, from a gentile.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage asked how far honoring parents must go; he answers with this story.

people.name: Dama ben Netina
people.about: A gentile of Ashkelon who gave up a huge profit rather than wake his father.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Teaches a different figure for the lost profit: eight hundred thousand.

terms.meaning: An apron-like garment worn by the High Priest, set with precious stones.
A completely red cow whose ashes were used to purify people who had become impure through contact with the dead. Such a cow was rare and valuable.
Gems listed among the gifts for the Tabernacle. The Gemara argues over whether the wording of the verse separates them from the earlier items in the list.

avodah_zarah-25b-9-9.note: Some students of Rabbi Akiva were traveling to Keziv when bandits met them and asked where they were going. The students said Akko, a place beyond their real destination. When they reached Keziv they parted from the bandits. The bandits asked whose students they were, and on hearing 'Rabbi Akiva's', said: Fortunate are Rabbi Akiva and his students, for no evil person has ever harmed them.
avodah_zarah-25b-9-9.why: The Gemara has just taught that a Jew traveling with a gentile who asks his destination should name a farther place, as Jacob told Esau he was going to Seir. This incident shows the advice working.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The teacher of the students in the story; the bandits praise him and them.

terms.meaning: Two towns; the students were really going to Keziv but named the more distant Akko.

avodah_zarah-25b-10-10.note: Rav Menashe was traveling to Bei Torta when thieves met him and asked where he was going. He said Pumbedita, which was farther away, and when he reached Bei Torta he parted from them. They said: You are a student of Yehuda the swindler! Rav Menashe answered, 'Do you know him?' and said, may it be God's will that these people be under Rav Yehuda's ban of excommunication. For twenty-two years their thefts failed. They all came to have the ban lifted, except one weaver, and a lion ate him.
avodah_zarah-25b-10-10.why: The Gemara has advised naming a farther destination to a dangerous traveling companion, with a story about Rabbi Akiva's students. This second case follows, and the Gemara then contrasts the Babylonian thieves, who cursed the teacher, with the bandits of the Land of Israel, who praised him.

people.name: Rav Menashe
people.about: A traveler who outwits thieves and calls a ban down on them when they insult his teacher.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rav Menashe's teacher, whom the thieves call 'Yehuda the swindler'.

terms.meaning: A formal ban by a Sage that cut a person off from the community; here it works as a curse on the thieves.
A weaver. The story ends with a saying that an impudent weaver has a year cut from his life.

avodah_zarah-27b-5-6.note: A snake bit ben Dama, the son of Rabbi Yishmael's sister. Ya'akov of the village of Sekhanya, a heretic, came to treat him, but Rabbi Yishmael would not let him. Ben Dama said: Rabbi Yishmael, my brother, let him treat me, and I will cite a verse from the Torah showing it is permitted. Before he could finish, he died. Rabbi Yishmael said over him: Fortunate are you, ben Dama, for your body is pure and your soul left in purity, and you did not break the words of your colleagues.
avodah_zarah-27b-5-6.why: The Gemara has said a Jew may be treated by a gentile healer when he would otherwise surely die. It raises this baraita as an objection, since ben Dama was refused a heretic's treatment even in mortal danger; the Gemara answers that heresy is different, because it can draw a person after it.

people.name: ben Dama
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yishmael's sister; bitten by a snake, he dies before he can argue for being treated.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Ben Dama's uncle, who forbids the heretic to treat him and praises him after his death.

people.name: Ya'akov of the village of Sekhanya
people.about: A heretic, described as a disciple of Jesus the Nazarene, who comes to heal ben Dama.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted in the Gemara.
Here, a Jew who has adopted a different faith; the Sages feared his influence more than a gentile's.

terms.term: who breaks through a fence, a snake shall bite him
terms.meaning: A verse from Ecclesiastes, read by the Sages as a warning that one who ignores their rulings will be punished.

avodah_zarah-28a-4-4.note: Rabbi Yohanan suffered from tzafdina, a disease of the gums and teeth, and went to a gentile noblewoman known as a healer. She treated him on Thursday and Friday, and he asked what he should do on Shabbat, when he could not come. She made him swear not to reveal her remedy, and he swore: 'To the God of Israel I will not reveal it.' She told him the cure, and the next day he went out and taught it publicly.
avodah_zarah-28a-4-4.why: The Gemara is asking whether a mouth or gum ailment counts as an internal illness, for which Shabbat may be broken to treat it. Rabbi Yohanan's Shabbat treatment is offered as proof, then set aside because tzafdina spreads to the intestines.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A leading Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, head of the academy in Tiberias.

terms.meaning: A disease of the gums and teeth that the Gemara says begins in the mouth and spreads to the intestines; its sign is bleeding between the teeth.
A Roman noblewoman; here a non-Jewish woman known as a healer.
The Jewish Sabbath, from Friday evening to Saturday night, when many kinds of work, including preparing most medicines, are forbidden.

avodah_zarah-28a-8-8.note: Abaye tells of his own illness of the gums. He tried all the remedies the Sages had just listed and was not cured, until a certain Arab told him: take olive seeds less than one-third ripe, burn them on a new hoe, and press them along the gums. He did this and was cured.
avodah_zarah-28a-8-8.why: The Gemara is discussing tzafdina, the gum disease for which a gentile matron treated Rabbi Yohanan, and two Sages have just named her remedy. Abaye adds that none of these worked for him and gives the cure that did.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who suffered from the gum disease and was cured by an Arab's remedy.

terms.meaning: A disease of the gums, in which blood flows from the teeth; the Gemara counts it as dangerous.

avodah_zarah-28a-10-10.note: Ya'akov the heretic put a salve on Rabbi Abbahu's leg that was really a poison. Had Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi not licked his leg to draw it out, the leg would have had to be cut off.
avodah_zarah-28a-10-10.why: The Gemara explained that Rabbi Yohanan could be treated by a gentile because no one would dare kill an important person. It cites this case as an objection, since Rabbi Abbahu was important too; it answers that heretics are willing to die in order to harm Jews.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: An important Sage whose leg a heretic tried to poison under the guise of treatment.

people.name: Ya'akov the heretic
people.about: The healer who put poison on Rabbi Abbahu's leg.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: One of the two Sages who licked the poison from Rabbi Abbahu's leg.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: One of the two Sages who licked the poison from Rabbi Abbahu's leg.

terms.meaning: Here, a Jew who has adopted a different faith and is hostile to the Sages.

avodah_zarah-28b-9-9.note: Rav Yehuda permitted someone to put blue eye shadow on an eye on Shabbat. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda said that anyone who follows Yehuda's ruling desecrates Shabbat. Later Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda himself had pain in his eye and sent to ask Rav Yehuda whether he could treat it on Shabbat. Rav Yehuda sent back: for everyone else it is permitted; for you it is forbidden.
avodah_zarah-28b-9-9.why: The Gemara has quoted Rav that an eye in danger may be treated with eye shadow on Shabbat, and Rav Yehuda's view that even grinding and carrying it through a public place is allowed. This story shows Rav Yehuda ruling that way and being challenged for it.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who permitted treating an eye on Shabbat and refused the leniency to the man who mocked it.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who said following Rav Yehuda desecrates Shabbat, then needed the ruling himself.

terms.meaning: A powder applied to the eye as a medicine; preparing and applying it would normally be forbidden on Shabbat.
The Sabbath, on which many kinds of work, including some medical treatment, are forbidden unless life is in danger.

avodah_zarah-28b-10-10.note: Rav Yehuda defends his ruling: it came from Mar Shmuel. A maidservant in Mar Shmuel's house had an infected eye on Shabbat. She screamed, but no one attended to her, and her eye burst. The next day Mar Shmuel went out and taught that an eye in danger may be treated with eye shadow on Shabbat, because the tendons of the eye are tied to the heart.
avodah_zarah-28b-10-10.why: Rav Yehuda had permitted treating an eye on Shabbat and refused the leniency to Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, who mocked it. Here he shows his ruling was not his own invention. The Gemara then asks which eye ailments count as dangerous.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Tells this story to show his ruling came from his teacher, Mar Shmuel.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The Sage in whose house the maidservant lost her eye; he then taught the leniency.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, on which treatment that involves forbidden work is allowed only when life is in danger.
An eye so badly affected that it may burst or come out of its socket.

avodah_zarah-29a-5-5.note: Rav Aha, son of Rava, ground the herbs of a remedy together and drank a handful. Rav Ashi ground each herb separately and took a pinch of each between his thumb and little finger. Rav Pappa said he tried all these remedies and was not healed, until a certain Arab told him: fill a new jug with water, put a ladle of honey in it overnight under the stars, and drink it the next day. He did this and was healed.
avodah_zarah-29a-5-5.why: The Gemara has listed a mixture of six herbs as the cure for bent ribs near the heart, and the drinks to take it with for different ailments. These Sages report how they actually took it, and what finally worked.

people.name: Rav Aha, son of Rava
people.about: Ground all the herbs together and drank a handful.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Ground each herb separately and took a pinch of each.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Tried all these remedies without success and was healed by an Arab's honey-water cure.

avodah_zarah-29a-10-10.note: Rav Hana bar Bizna was having his hair cut by a gentile in a side street of Neharde'a. The barber said to him: Hana, Hana, your throat is appealing to the razor. Rav Hana bar Bizna said: I have this coming to me, for I went against the ruling of Rabbi Meir.
avodah_zarah-29a-10-10.why: The mishna forbids having one's hair cut by a gentile; Rabbi Meir forbids it anywhere, and the Rabbis allow it in public. The Gemara uses this story to ask whether a side street counts as public, and answers that one crowded with people does.

people.name: Rav Hana bar Bizna
people.about: A Sage who let a gentile cut his hair and was menaced by the barber.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage whose ruling forbids being shaved by a gentile in any place.

terms.meaning: A city in Babylonia with a large Jewish community.

avodah_zarah-30a-8-8.note: Rabbi Yannai, or some say bar Hadaya, was in Bei Akhborei with others, drinking diluted wine. Some wine was left in the container, and they covered it with a cloth. They then saw a snake carry water in its mouth and pour it through the cloth until the container filled and the wine rose above the cloth, and the snake drank it.
avodah_zarah-30a-8-8.why: The Gemara is asking whether wine left uncovered must be thrown out for fear a snake drank from it, and has just argued that a snake will not risk its life for diluted wine. This story challenges that; the Sages reply that a snake drinks only wine it diluted itself.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: A Sage present when the snake drank the wine; some say it was bar Hadaya.

people.name: bar Hadaya
people.about: Named in another version as the one who was in Bei Akhborei.

terms.meaning: Wine mixed with water, as wine was usually drunk in the ancient world.
The rule that a drink left uncovered may not be drunk, in case a snake drank from it and left venom.

avodah_zarah-30b-5-5.note: Nine people drank from a barrel that had been left uncovered and did not die. A tenth drank from it and died. Rabbi Yirmeya said this shows venom that sinks.
avodah_zarah-30b-5-5.why: Rav Safra has taught that a young snake's venom sinks to the bottom of a liquid. The Gemara asks what rule this affects and quotes a baraita: even if nine have drunk safely from an uncovered barrel, a tenth may not, and this incident is its proof.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Explains the tenth drinker's death as venom that had sunk to the bottom.

terms.meaning: According to the discussion, the venom of a young snake sinks to the bottom of a liquid, so the first drinkers may be unharmed.

avodah_zarah-30b-6-6.note: Nine people ate from a melon that had been left uncovered and did not die. A tenth ate from it and died. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said this shows venom that sinks.
avodah_zarah-30b-6-6.why: After the case of the uncovered barrel, where the tenth drinker died, the Gemara applies the same rule to food: even if nine have eaten safely from an uncovered melon, a tenth may not, and this incident is the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply 'Rabbi'; he explains the death as venom that had sunk.

terms.meaning: According to the discussion, a young snake's venom sinks deep, so the first ones to eat may be unharmed.

avodah_zarah-33a-11-11.note: Bar Adi the Arab seized some wineskins from Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef, put wine in them, and gave them back. Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef asked in the study hall what to do. Rabbi Yirmeya told him that Rabbi Ami had ruled in practice: fill them with water for three days and pour it out. Rava added that the water must be poured out and replaced every twenty-four hours.
avodah_zarah-33a-11-11.why: The Gemara is discussing vessels that have absorbed a gentile's wine, which Jews may not use. This case gives the method for making such wineskins usable, and the Gemara next asks whether it also applies to the gentiles' own wineskins and to jugs.

people.name: Bar Adi the Arab
people.about: Seized Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef's wineskins, filled them with wine, and returned them.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: Owner of the wineskins, who asked in the study hall how to make them usable.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Answers with a practical ruling he received from Rabbi Ami.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Ruled that such wineskins be filled with water for three days.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Adds that the water must be changed every twenty-four hours.

terms.meaning: Wine handled by non-Jews, which the Sages forbade for fear it had been poured out to idols; vessels that absorbed it were also forbidden.

avodah_zarah-33b-4-4.note: Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna had vessels made of dung that had held gentile wine. To clean them, he filled them with water and set them in the sun, and they burst. Rabbi Abba told him: you have made them forbidden to you forever. The Sages said to fill them with water; did they say to put them in the sun?
avodah_zarah-33b-4-4.why: The Gemara is going through ways to make vessels that held gentile wine usable again, such as soaking in water or firing in a furnace. This story shows the water method misapplied, and the Gemara goes on to vessels that can never be made usable.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna
people.about: Owner of the dung vessels, which burst when he left them full of water in the sun.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Teases him that he has made the vessels forbidden forever.

terms.meaning: Wine handled by non-Jews, which the Sages forbade; vessels that absorbed it had to be cleaned before a Jew could use them.

avodah_zarah-33b-6-6.note: Parzak, of the vizier's household, seized some containers from the Jews of Pumbedita, put wine in them, and gave them back. The owners asked Rav Yehuda what to do. He said these were vessels not used for long storage, so they need only be rinsed in water and they are permitted.
avodah_zarah-33b-6-6.why: The Gemara is listing which vessels that held gentile wine can be made usable, and how. This ruling sets a short-use vessel apart, needing only rinsing, and is followed by other kinds of jugs that absorb little and need only rinsing.

people.name: Parzak
people.about: A man of the vizier's household who seized the vessels and put wine in them.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rules that the returned vessels need only be rinsed.

terms.meaning: Wine handled by non-Jews, which the Sages forbade; vessels that absorbed it had to be cleaned before a Jew could use them.
A high official of the ruling government.

avodah_zarah-34b-3-4.note: A boat carrying fish stew came to the port of Akko, and Rabbi Abba from Akko set guards over it. Rava asked him who had guarded it until now. Rabbi Abba answered that there was nothing to fear: where the stew was made, wine cost four times as much as fish stew, so no one would mix wine into it. Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Zeira whether the boat might have come by way of Tyre, where wine is cheap. Rabbi Zeira said that route had obstacles and melted snow.
avodah_zarah-34b-3-4.why: The mishna forbids gentile fish stew, and a baraita permits it when made by an expert; the worry is that wine was mixed in. This case applies that worry to stew shipped from abroad.

people.name: Rabbi Abba from Akko
people.about: Set guards over the fish stew boat once it reached port.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Asks who guarded the stew before it arrived.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Asks whether the boat came by way of Tyre, where wine is cheap.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Answers that the Tyre route was blocked by obstacles and melted snow.

terms.meaning: A salty fish sauce; the Sages suspected gentile makers of adding wine to it, which would make it forbidden.
A measure of liquid and a coin; the prices show that wine was much dearer than fish stew.

avodah_zarah-35b-15-16.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once went out to the field, and a gentile brought him a large loaf baked in a big baker's oven. He said: How fine this bread is! What did the Sages see to forbid it? The Gemara explains that he meant: why forbid it even in the field? People who heard of this thought he had permitted gentile bread, but he had not.
avodah_zarah-35b-15-16.why: Rabbi Yohanan has said that, unlike oil, gentile bread was never permitted by a court, implying someone thought it was. This report shows where that idea came from and why it was mistaken.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply 'Rabbi'; he admires a gentile's bread in the field and asks why it was forbidden there.

terms.meaning: The Sages forbade bread baked by non-Jews, out of concern that eating together would lead to intermarriage.
A measure of volume, here describing a very large loaf.

avodah_zarah-35b-17-17.note: Rav Yosef, or some say Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, tells the incident differently. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi came to a certain place and saw that bread was scarce for the students. He asked: Is there no baker here? People thought he meant a gentile baker, but he meant only a Jewish baker.
avodah_zarah-35b-17-17.why: The Gemara is explaining why people believed gentile bread had been permitted, though Rabbi Yohanan says no court ever permitted it. This is a second version of the incident behind that belief.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Gives this version of the incident; some say it was Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: Named in another version as the one who tells it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply 'Rabbi'; he asks for a baker when the students are short of bread.

terms.meaning: A professional baker who bakes bread for sale.

avodah_zarah-37a-2-3.note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia was walking, leaning on the shoulder of his attendant Rabbi Simlai, and told him: you missed the study hall last night, when we permitted the oil of gentiles. Simlai replied that in their days he would permit gentiles' bread as well. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia answered that people would then call them a permissive court, as they had called Rabbi Yosei ben Yo'ezer 'Yosef the Permissive' for his three lenient rulings. Simlai pointed out that Yosei had permitted three things, Rabbi Yehuda Nesia only one, so another would make just two. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia said he had already permitted another: according to Shmuel, it was his court that allowed a woman to remarry under a certain conditional bill of divorce.
avodah_zarah-37a-2-3.why: The exchange is the Gemara's record that Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's court permitted gentiles' oil; the Gemara then turns aside to examine that same court's ruling on the conditional bill of divorce.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The head of the court that permitted the oil of gentiles.

people.name: Rabbi Simlai
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's attendant, who was absent from the study hall the night the oil was permitted.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Yo'ezer of Tzereida
people.about: An earlier Sage nicknamed 'Yosef the Permissive' for three lenient rulings.

terms.meaning: Olive oil made by non-Jews, which had been forbidden to Jews until this court permitted it.
The document a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. Here it was given on a condition, and the husband died before the condition could be tested.
The early collection of rabbinic teachings on which the Gemara comments.

avodah_zarah-38b-5-5.note: Rabbi Hiyya of Parva visited the home of the Exilarch, and the household asked him whether an egg roasted by a gentile may be eaten. He answered that Hizkiyya and bar Kappara permit it while Rabbi Yohanan forbids it, and one Sage's view does not stand against two. Rav Zevid told them not to listen to him, because Abaye had said the law follows Rabbi Yohanan. They gave Rav Zevid a cup of spiced vinegar to drink, and he died.
avodah_zarah-38b-5-5.why: The Gemara has just recorded the dispute over salted fish and roasted eggs prepared by gentiles; this visit shows the dispute being decided in practice, and the teaching that follows states plainly that a gentile's roasted egg is forbidden.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya of Parva
people.about: A visiting Sage asked about the roasted egg; he ruled that it is permitted, following the majority.

people.name: Rav Zevid
people.about: Told the household not to listen, citing Abaye's ruling for Rabbi Yohanan; he died after drinking the vinegar they gave him.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage whose ruling Rav Zevid quotes: the law follows Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who forbids a gentile's roasted egg.

people.name: Hizkiyya
people.about: Sage who, with bar Kappara, permits a gentile's roasted egg.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who kept a large household.
Jewish law; the binding ruling on a question.

avodah_zarah-39a-8-8.note: Two Sages were brought fish that looked like forbidden kinds. In Ginzak, Rabbi Akiva was shown a fish resembling a non-kosher sea creature; he shut it in a basket, saw that it shed scales as it struggled, and permitted it. In Tamduria, Rav Ashi was shown a fish that looked like an eel; he held it up to the daylight, saw thin scales on it, and permitted it.
avodah_zarah-39a-8-8.why: The Gemara has been listing which fish are permitted and which forbidden; these visits show Sages settling doubtful cases by looking for scales, and the run of similar incidents continues afterward.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Sage who, in Ginzak, examined a doubtful fish in a basket and permitted it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who, in Tamduria, held a fish to the light and permitted it.

terms.meaning: Declared the fish kosher, fit for Jews to eat. A fish needs scales to be kosher, so finding scales settled the doubt.

avodah_zarah-39a-9-9.note: Rav Ashi came to a certain place where he was served a fish that looked like a shefarnuna. He put it in a white vessel, saw the scales it shed, and permitted it. Rabba bar bar Hana came to Akra DeAgma and was served tzahanta, a dish of small fish, and heard a man call it batei, the name of a non-kosher sea creature. He concluded there was something non-kosher in it and did not eat. In the morning he examined the dish, found a non-kosher substance in it, and applied to himself the verse: 'No sin shall befall the righteous.'
avodah_zarah-39a-9-9.why: The Gemara is gathering cases of Sages deciding whether an unfamiliar fish was kosher, mostly by looking for scales; Rabba bar bar Hana's case adds a different kind of evidence, a name overheard at the table.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who checks a doubtful fish for scales and permits it.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who refuses a dish because of what a man called it, and turns out to be right.

terms.meaning: A fish is kosher only if it has fins and scales, so finding scales settles whether a doubtful fish may be eaten.
A kind of fish the Gemara has just called permitted.
Food that Jewish law forbids to be eaten.

avodah_zarah-39a-12-12.note: A non-Jewish slave belonging to Rabbi Levi used to sell hiltit, a pungent spice, and people bought from him because his master was a Sage. When Rabbi Levi died, people came to Rabbi Yohanan and asked whether they could still buy from the slave. He answered that the slave of a haver is like a haver himself, so they could.
avodah_zarah-39a-12-12.why: The mishna forbids eating hiltit from a gentile because it is cut with a knife that may carry non-kosher residue. This case shows when it may be bought anyway, and opens a discussion of trusting the household of a careful observer.

people.name: Rabbi Levi
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, whose slave sold spices.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A leading Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, head of the academy in Tiberias.

terms.meaning: Asafoetida, a sharp-tasting plant resin used as a spice and medicine. It was sliced with a knife, which raised concern about non-kosher residue.
Literally 'associate': a person who has committed to careful observance of the laws of tithes and ritual purity, and whose food could therefore be trusted.

avodah_zarah-39a-13-14.note: Rav Huna bar Minyumi bought sky-blue dye from the household (the wife) of Rav Amram the pious and asked Rav Yosef whether he could rely on her; Rav Yosef did not know. Hanan the tailor met Rav Huna and said: how could poor Yosef know? It happened to me: I bought dye from the wife of Rabena'a, brother of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, and Rav Mattana did not know either. Then Rav Yehuda of Hagronya told me, "You have fallen into my hand," and quoted Shmuel: the wife of a haver is like a haver herself.
avodah_zarah-39a-13-14.why: Rabbi Yohanan has just ruled that the slave of a haver is trusted like a haver; this story extends the same trust to his wife, and the Gemara then notes a teaching of the Sages that says both.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Minyumi
people.about: Bought sky-blue dye from Rav Amram's wife and sought a ruling on it.

people.name: Rav Amram the pious
people.about: Sage from whose household the dye was bought.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who did not know the answer to Rav Huna's question.

people.name: Hanan the tailor
people.about: Told Rav Huna of his own similar case and how it was answered.

people.name: Rav Yehuda of Hagronya
people.about: Answered Hanan, quoting Shmuel that a haver's wife is trusted like a haver.

terms.meaning: The blue dye required for one thread of ritual fringes. It was easy to counterfeit, so it could be bought only from a trusted seller.
A member of a fellowship committed to careful observance, especially of purity and tithing laws, and so trusted on such matters.

avodah_zarah-39a-17-17.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar told of a woman who was married to a haver and used to tie his phylacteries on his hand. Later she married a tax collector, and she used to tie his tax-seals on his hand.
avodah_zarah-39a-17-17.why: Rabbi Meir has said that a haver's wife who remarries an ordinary man need not take on the haver's commitments anew, and Rabbi Yehuda disagrees; this case backs Rabbi Yehuda, showing a wife follows the ways of whoever she is married to.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: Sage who tells the incident of the woman.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage who rules that such people must take on the haver's commitments from the start.

terms.meaning: A member of a fellowship committed to careful observance, especially of purity and tithing laws.
Tefillin: small leather boxes containing Torah verses, bound on the arm and head during weekday prayer.
Seals or tags a tax collector used in his work, here tied on his hand the way phylacteries are.

avodah_zarah-40a-5-5.note: A ship carrying tzahanta, a small-fish dish, came to Sikhra. Rav Huna bar Hinnana went out, saw scales among the fish, and permitted it. Rava objected: who permits in such a case, in a place where scales are common? Shofar blasts went out from Rava's court forbidding the fish, and shofar blasts went out from Rav Huna bar Hinnana's court permitting it.
avodah_zarah-40a-5-5.why: The Gemara is asking when fish brine and pieces of fish may be trusted, and Rav Pappa requires every fish to be recognizable; after this case the Gemara gives two versions of whether Rav Huna bar Hinnana permitted only the brine or the fish themselves.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hinnana
people.about: Sage who saw scales on the ship's fish and permitted them.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who objected and forbade the fish.

terms.meaning: A dish made from small fish.
Blowing the shofar (ram's horn) was how a court publicly announced its ruling.

avodah_zarah-40b-7-8.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had stomach pain and asked whether anyone knew if gentiles' apple wine is permitted. Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei said that his father once had stomach pain, was brought gentiles' apple wine seventy years old, drank it and was cured. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: you had all this in your hand and let me suffer! They searched and found a gentile with three hundred jugs of seventy-year-old apple wine. He drank and was cured, and said: Blessed is the Omnipresent who delivered His world to keepers.
avodah_zarah-40b-7-8.why: A teaching of the Sages has just said that gentiles' apple wine from a storehouse is permitted, while apple wine sold in the market is forbidden because grape wine may be mixed in; this story shows the leniency relied on.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Sage, called simply Rabbi, who needed apple wine for his stomach pain.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that his father had drunk gentiles' apple wine as a cure.

terms.meaning: A name for God.
A drink made from apples. Unlike grape wine, it is not used in idol worship, so the question was only whether grape wine had been mixed in.

avodah_zarah-41b-14-14.note: Rabbi Yehuda told of a case in the town of Rimon: the maidservant of a violent man threw a stillborn baby into a pit. A priest came and looked into the pit to see whether it was male or female. The case came before the Sages, and they ruled the priest ritually pure, because martens and polecats are common there.
avodah_zarah-41b-14-14.why: The Gemara has argued that an uncertainty cannot override a certainty; this case is raised as an objection, since the Sages let the doubt that animals dragged the body away outweigh the certainty that it was thrown in.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage who reports the case.

people.name: a priest
people.about: Looked into the pit; a priest must avoid the impurity of a corpse.

terms.meaning: Not made impure. A priest who is under the same roof or over a corpse becomes impure and is barred from Temple service and holy food.
Small animals that might have dragged the body out of the pit before the priest arrived.

avodah_zarah-43a-6-6.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi recalled walking on the road behind Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who found a ring bearing the figure of a dragon. He met a gentile boy and said nothing to him. Then he met an adult gentile and told him to revoke the ring's idolatrous status, but the man would not. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar slapped him, and he revoked it.
avodah_zarah-43a-6-6.why: The Sages have just defined the dragon figure that marks an object as idolatrous; from this incident the Gemara learns that a gentile can revoke another's idol, that only one who understands idol worship can do so, and that it works even against his will.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Passes on the account in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Was walking with Rabbi Elazar HaKappar and tells what happened.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
people.about: Found the ring and made an adult gentile revoke its status.

terms.meaning: To cancel an object's status as an idol, done by a gentile through an act of disrespect toward it; after that a Jew may use it.
An image the Sages treat as a sign that an object was made for idol worship.

avodah_zarah-43a-13-15.note: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda taught that one may not make even a wooden candelabrum like the Temple's, as the Hasmoneans made one of wood. The Rabbis answered that the Hasmoneans' candelabrum was not wood: its branches were iron spits covered with tin. When they grew richer they made it of silver, and when they grew richer still, of gold.
avodah_zarah-43a-13-15.why: Abaye cites this teaching for his view that the Torah bans making only copies that can truly reproduce their model, such as a seven-branched candelabrum, which is why figures of the moon were allowed.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who holds that even a wooden copy of the Temple candelabrum is forbidden.

terms.meaning: The seven-branched lampstand (menorah) that stood in the Temple. A private copy with seven lamps is forbidden.
The family of priests who ruled Judea and purified the Temple; the text says they first had to make the candelabrum from poor materials.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

avodah_zarah-50a-7-8.note: The house of King Yannai was destroyed, and gentiles set up stones to the god Mercury in it. Later, other gentiles who did not worship Mercury took the stones and paved paths and streets with them. Some Rabbis kept off those paths and others did not. Rabbi Yohanan said: the son of holy ones walks on them, and should we keep away? The Gemara explains that this was Rabbi Menahem son of Rabbi Simai, called so because he would not even look at the image on a coin.
avodah_zarah-50a-7-8.why: The Gemara has been defining which stones count as part of a Mercury pile; after the story it gives the reasoning on each side, whether an idolatrous offering can ever lose its forbidden status, or whether stones are not offerings at all.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: King whose ruined house the gentiles used.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who argued against avoiding the paved paths.

people.name: Rabbi Menahem son of Rabbi Simai
people.about: Called the son of holy ones; he walked on the paths, though he would not even look at the image on a coin.

terms.meaning: A Roman god worshipped by adding stones to a heap or by throwing stones at it; the stones count as forbidden idol offerings.

avodah_zarah-54b-17-21.note: A philosopher asked Rabban Gamliel: your Torah calls God a jealous God, so why is He jealous of idol worshippers but not of the idol itself? Rabban Gamliel told a parable of a king whose son named his dog after his father and swore by it: the king is angry with the son, not the dog. The philosopher said the idol has real power: when his city burned, only its temple survived. Rabban Gamliel answered with a king who wages war on the living, not the dead. Then let God destroy it, said the philosopher. Rabban Gamliel replied that people worship the sun, moon, stars and rivers: should God destroy His world because of fools? He cited a verse from Zephaniah: people worship humans too, so must humanity be cut off?
avodah_zarah-54b-17-21.why: The Gemara has just taught that the world follows its course and sinners will be judged later, even when God seems to allow wrongdoing; this exchange carries the theme to idols, which God lets stand.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Sage who answers the philosopher's questions with parables and a verse.

people.name: a philosopher
people.about: A non-Jewish thinker who challenges Rabban Gamliel about God's jealousy and idols.

terms.meaning: A short illustrative tale, here about a king, used to explain how God acts.
A phrase from Deuteronomy describing God's response to idol worship.

avodah_zarah-56b-4-4.note: In Neharde'a a Jew and a gentile trod grapes together to make wine, and Shmuel put off ruling on that wine for three Festivals, when the Sages gathered. The Gemara asks why. It rejects the idea that he hoped to find a teacher who sided with Rabbi Natan, which would forbid even profiting from the wine, since Rabbi Natan forbids only a gentile's touch by hand. Rather, says the Gemara, he hoped to find one who sided with Rabbi Shimon, so he could permit the wine even for drinking. The text does not say how he finally ruled.
avodah_zarah-56b-4-4.why: A gifted child has just ruled that a Jew may tread grapes alongside a gentile, since a foot's touch does not make wine a libation; Shmuel's long hesitation over a real case shows the question was far from simple.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage who delayed his ruling on the wine for three Festivals.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: Sage who forbids wine a gentile measured by hand but permits it by foot.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Sage who permits wine a gentile touched without meaning to offer it.

terms.meaning: The pilgrimage holidays, when Sages gathered and questions could be discussed.
A Sage of the earlier period whose teachings carry authority; Shmuel sought one supporting a ruling.
Wine poured out in idol worship. Wine a gentile may have offered this way is forbidden to Jews.

avodah_zarah-57a-2-3.note: In Biram a gentile climbing down a palm tree with a palm branch touched some wine with the tip of the branch, without meaning to. Rav permitted the owners to sell the wine to gentiles. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi asked him: didn't you, Master, say that even a one-day-old gentile baby makes wine a libation by touching it? Rav answered: I said it forbids drinking the wine; did I say it forbids benefit from it?
avodah_zarah-57a-2-3.why: The Gemara has been asking what a gentile's unintended touch does to wine, in Shmuel's case; Rav's ruling separates drinking from profiting, and the Gemara then turns to examine his statement about the baby.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who let the wine be sold to gentiles.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: With Rav Asi, challenged Rav using his own statement.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: With Rav Kahana, challenged Rav using his own statement.

terms.meaning: Wine poured out in idol worship. Wine a gentile may have offered this way is forbidden to Jews.
Making any use or profit of something, such as selling it, as opposed to eating or drinking it.

avodah_zarah-57b-6-7.note: In Mehoza a gentile walked into a Jew's shop and asked for wine. Told there was none, he put his hand in a bucket of wine, stirred it, and said: isn't this wine? In anger the shopkeeper threw it into a barrel. Rava permitted selling the barrel to gentiles; Rav Huna bar Hinnana and Rav Huna son of Rav Nahman forbade it, and each court announced its ruling with shofar blasts. When Rav Huna son of Rav Nahman came to Mehoza, Rava had his attendant shut the gates so they would not be disturbed. Asked about such a case, Rava said even benefit is forbidden; challenged, he said he had permitted the barrel except for the value of the stirred wine.
avodah_zarah-57b-6-7.why: The Gemara is asking whether a gentile's touch without intent to worship forbids wine; afterward Rava recalls that Abaye pressed him with Shmuel's and Rabbi Yohanan's rulings forbidding stirred wine, and with a teaching of the Sages.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage in Mehoza who permitted the barrel to be sold to gentiles.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hinnana
