people.about: Sage who disagreed with Rava and forbade the sale.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage who forbade the sale and came to Mehoza to question Rava.

people.name: Rav Elyakim
people.about: Rava's attendant, told to shut the gates.

terms.meaning: Blowing the shofar (ram's horn) was how a court publicly announced its ruling.
Wine poured out in idol worship. Wine a gentile may have offered this way is forbidden to Jews.
Making any use or profit of something, such as selling it, as opposed to drinking it.

avodah_zarah-58a-6-6.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza and Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai were sitting and drinking wine when a man came by, and they asked him to pour for them. After he poured, it turned out he was a gentile. One of the two Sages forbade the wine even for any benefit, while the other allowed it even for drinking. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said both were right: one assumed the gentile thought such great Sages must be drinking wine and might have poured it to an idol, the other that he assumed they were drinking liquor, since they would never ask a gentile to serve them wine.
avodah_zarah-58a-6-6.why: The Gemara has been debating how strictly to treat wine a gentile touched by accident, after Abaye refuted Rava's lenient view; this incident adds a case where the gentile's own assumptions decide whether he meant to offer it to an idol.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza
people.about: One of the two Sages drinking wine; one of them forbade it and one permitted it.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai
people.about: The other Sage drinking wine with Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: A Sage who later judged that both rulings were proper and explained each one.

terms.meaning: Offering wine to an idol by pouring it out. Wine a gentile may have poured for an idol was forbidden to Jews, even for selling.
Any use or profit from something, such as selling it, not only eating or drinking it.

avodah_zarah-58b-6-7.note: Reish Lakish came to Bozrah and saw Jews eating untithed produce, and he forbade it to them. He also saw Jews drinking water that gentiles bowed down to, and he forbade it too. He came before Rabbi Yohanan, who told him: while your coat is still on you, go back and retract. Bozrah is not the Bezer named in the Torah, so its produce needs no tithing, and public water is not made forbidden. The text does not say whether he went back.
avodah_zarah-58b-6-7.why: The Gemara has just told of Rabbi Yirmeya forbidding diluted wine on a visit to Savta; afterward it notes that Rabbi Yohanan's rule here, that public water cannot be made forbidden, matches what he taught elsewhere.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Sage who forbade produce and water to the Jews of Bozrah.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who told Reish Lakish to go back and retract both rulings.

terms.meaning: Crops grown in the Land of Israel from which the required portions for priests, Levites and the poor have not been set aside; eating them is forbidden.
A city named in the Torah as a city of refuge, in the land of Israel; Rabbi Yohanan says Bozrah is a different place.

avodah_zarah-59a-4-5.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba came to Gavla. He saw Jewish women pregnant by gentiles who had been circumcised but had not yet immersed for conversion, Jews drinking wine that gentiles had diluted, and Jews eating lupines that gentiles had cooked, and he said nothing to them. He came before Rabbi Yohanan, who told him: go and declare their children mamzerim, their wine forbidden as libation wine, and their lupines forbidden as food cooked by gentiles, because they are not people learned in Torah.
avodah_zarah-59a-4-5.why: The Gemara then explains each instruction by Rabbi Yohanan's own rulings: a convert needs both circumcision and immersion, a child of a gentile and a Jewish woman is a mamzer, and people unlearned in Torah need stricter fences.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: Sage who saw the practices in Gavla and said nothing.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who told him to declare all three forbidden.

terms.meaning: Dipping in a ritual bath, the final step of conversion; until then the man is still legally a gentile.
Children of a forbidden union, who may not marry ordinary Jews.
Wine that may have been poured out in idol worship, forbidden to Jews; here extended to wine a gentile diluted.
A rabbinic ban on certain foods cooked by non-Jews.

avodah_zarah-59b-1-1.note: An etrog fell into a barrel of wine, and a gentile jumped up to take it out. Rav Ashi told the people there: hold his hand so that he does not stir the wine, and tip the barrel until the wine has drained out.
avodah_zarah-59b-1-1.why: Rav Kahana has just ruled that a gentile should not be allowed to bring grapes to the winepress in the first place, as a fence; Rav Ashi's instruction is another way of keeping a gentile's touch from making a Jew's wine forbidden.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who told the bystanders how to save the wine.

terms.meaning: A citron, the fruit used in the Sukkot festival.
A gentile's stirring of wine is treated like touching it in worship, which can make it forbidden to Jews.

avodah_zarah-60a-7-7.note: A barrel of wine split open lengthwise from top to bottom, and a gentile jumped up and wrapped his arms around it to keep the wine from spilling. Rafram bar Pappa (some say Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua) ruled that the wine could be sold to gentiles, though not drunk by Jews.
avodah_zarah-60a-7-7.why: The Gemara is discussing when a gentile's indirect force makes wine forbidden. It adds that if the barrel had split widthwise, the gentile would only be holding it together like a weight, and the wine could even be drunk.

people.name: Rafram bar Pappa
people.about: The Sage who ruled the wine could be sold to gentiles; some attribute the ruling to Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Named as the alternative source of the same ruling.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. Here the concern is that a gentile might pour out or dedicate wine as an offering to an idol, which would make it forbidden to Jews.

avodah_zarah-62b-3-3.note: A man rented out his ship to carry ordinary gentile wine, and was paid in wheat. He came to Rav Hisda to ask whether he could keep it. Rav Hisda told him: go burn it and bury it in a graveyard.
avodah_zarah-62b-3-3.why: The Sages had asked whether a Jew's wage for working with ordinary gentile wine is forbidden, like a wage for idolatrous wine. Rav Hisda's ruling shows it is; the Gemara then asks why the wheat had to be both burned and buried.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage the ship owner consulted; he ordered the wheat burned and buried.

terms.meaning: Ordinary wine belonging to non-Jews that was not known to have been offered to an idol. The Sages still forbade Jews to drink it or profit from it.

avodah_zarah-62b-7-7.note: The students of Rabbi Yannai's school borrowed produce of the Sabbatical Year from poor people and paid them back in the eighth year. People reported this to Rabbi Yohanan, worried it was forbidden trading in that produce. Rabbi Yohanan said they were acting properly.
avodah_zarah-62b-7-7.why: The Gemara then compares this to a payment given to a prostitute well before or after the act, which is not treated as her fee; in the same way, repaying the borrowed produce after time has passed is not counted as trading.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: The head of the school whose students borrowed the produce.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who was told about the loans and approved them.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year the land of Israel rests. Produce that grows that year is holy in a special way: it is shared freely and may not be bought and sold as ordinary goods.

avodah_zarah-64b-15-15.note: Rav Yehuda sent a gift to a gentile named Avidarna on his people's festival day, saying he knew Avidarna did not worship idols. Rav Yosef challenged him: a teaching says a resident non-Jew counts as such only if he accepted before three Jews not to worship idols, and Avidarna had not. Rav Yehuda answered that this teaching only concerns the duty to support such a person.
avodah_zarah-64b-15-15.why: The Gemara has just discussed how far a resident non-Jew is treated like any gentile. Giving gifts to idol worshippers on their festivals is forbidden, so the story asks whether a gentile known not to worship idols counts as one.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who sent the festival gift and defended doing so.

people.name: Avidarna
people.about: A gentile who received the gift; Rav Yehuda says he does not worship idols.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who objected to the gift.

terms.meaning: A resident non-Jew: a gentile who has formally renounced idol worship and lives among Jews, without converting.
Literally 'fellows': Jews trusted for their careful observance, here serving as witnesses to the gentile's commitment.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

avodah_zarah-65a-2-3.note: Rava brought a festival gift to bar Sheshakh, a minister he believed did not worship idols, and found him sitting up to his neck in rose water with naked prostitutes standing before him. Bar Sheshakh asked whether Jews would have anything like this in the World-to-Come. Rava said theirs would be better, because there they would not live in fear of the government. Bar Sheshakh scoffed that he feared no one, but just then a royal officer summoned him to the king. Leaving, he said, 'May any eye that wishes to see evil upon you burst.' Rava said 'Amen', and bar Sheshakh's eye burst.
avodah_zarah-65a-2-3.why: It follows Rav Yehuda's gift to Avidarna, a second case of a Sage giving a gentile a festival gift on the grounds that he did not worship idols. Afterward Rav Pappi and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak suggest verses Rava could have answered with.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who brought the gift and answered bar Sheshakh's boast.

people.name: bar Sheshakh
people.about: A powerful minister who received Rava's gift and mocked the Jews' World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: The life of reward after this world, or the age to come, as Jewish tradition describes it.
A royal officer or messenger, sent here to fetch bar Sheshakh to the king.

avodah_zarah-65a-15-15.note: The father of Rav Aha, son of Rav Ika, would pour wine he sold to gentiles into their wineskins and ferry them across the river, and they paid him with the jugs the wine had been stored in. People came and told Abaye. Abaye said that when he did the work, he was working with permitted wine.
avodah_zarah-65a-15-15.why: The discussion concerns when a Jew's wage for work involving gentile wine is forbidden. The Gemara goes on to ask how the father avoided working with forbidden wine, since he ferried it and wanted the wineskins not to tear.

people.name: Rav Ika
people.about: Father of Rav Aha; he sold and ferried wine to gentiles and was paid in jugs.

people.name: Rav Aha
people.about: Son of Rav Ika, named only to identify his father.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who was told about the arrangement and ruled it permitted.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. Here the concern is that a gentile might pour out or dedicate wine as an offering to an idol, which would make it forbidden to Jews.

avodah_zarah-65b-5-5.note: Boethus ben Zunen was carrying dried figs on a ship when a barrel of wine used for idol worship broke and spilled on them. The case came before the Sages, and they ruled the figs permitted.
avodah_zarah-65b-5-5.why: The Mishna told this incident right after saying figs are forbidden if wine flavors them. The Gemara explains that the Mishna is incomplete: wine that spoils the taste does not forbid, and this incident illustrates that rule.

people.name: Boethus ben Zunen
people.about: A man shipping dried figs, onto which forbidden wine spilled.

terms.meaning: Wine poured out as an offering to an idol. Jews may not drink it or profit from it; wine a gentile may have touched or moved is treated with suspicion of this.
When a forbidden food gives a taste to permitted food that makes it worse rather than better. The rule here is that such a mixture stays permitted.

avodah_zarah-65b-6-9.note: A barrel of wine used for idol worship fell on a heap of wheat, and Rava allowed the wheat to be sold to gentiles. Rabba bar Livai objected from a teaching that a garment with forbidden mixed fibers may not be sold to a gentile, lest he sell it on to a Jew; the same could happen with the wheat. Rava changed his ruling: the wheat could be ground, baked into bread and sold to gentiles, but not where Jews could see.
avodah_zarah-65b-6-9.why: The Mishna said wine spilled on grapes can be rinsed off. The Gemara next asks why rinsing did not work for the wheat, and Rav Pappa answers that wheat has slits, like cracked grapes.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the wheat and then revised his ruling.

people.name: Rabba bar Livai
people.about: The Sage who challenged Rava's first ruling.

terms.meaning: Wine poured out as an offering to an idol. Jews may not drink it or profit from it; wine a gentile may have touched or moved is treated with suspicion of this.
The Torah's ban on wearing cloth that mixes wool and linen.
A dead body with no one to bury it, which anyone who finds it must bury.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

avodah_zarah-68b-10-11.note: A mouse fell into a barrel of beer, and Rav declared the beer forbidden. The Sages asked Rav Sheshet whether this meant Rav held that a forbidden thing forbids even when its taste makes the food worse. Rav Sheshet said no: generally Rav permits such a case, but a mouse is a special case, because it is disgusting and people avoid it, yet the Torah forbids it anyway, so it forbids even when it spoils the taste.
avodah_zarah-68b-10-11.why: The discussion is about forbidden ingredients that worsen a food's flavor. The Sages then press Rav Sheshet: if a mouse is so stringent, why does a dried-out dead mouse not convey ritual impurity?

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who declared the beer forbidden.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: The Sage who explained Rav's ruling to the Sages.

terms.meaning: When a forbidden food gives a taste to permitted food that makes it worse. Usually such a mixture stays permitted.
A common Talmudic way of referring to God as the giver of the Torah.

avodah_zarah-70a-1-1.note: In a house where Jews stored wine, a gentile went in and locked the door on the Jew, but there was a crack in the door, and the gentile was found standing among the barrels. Rava ruled that barrels in view of the crack were permitted, since he would fear being seen, but barrels to either side of it were forbidden.
avodah_zarah-70a-1-1.why: It opens a run of Rava's rulings on gentiles left alone with Jewish wine, after his rulings about wine at a prostitute's table. The question in each is whether the gentile would have feared being seen.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled on which barrels remained permitted.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. Here the concern is that a gentile might pour out or dedicate wine as an offering to an idol, which would make it forbidden to Jews.

avodah_zarah-70a-2-2.note: A Jew lived upstairs and a gentile downstairs in a house where the Jew's wine was stored below. Hearing a quarrel, both went outside; the gentile came back first and locked the door on the Jew. Rava ruled the wine permitted: the gentile would think the Jew might also have come back early and be watching him from upstairs.
avodah_zarah-70a-2-2.why: It is one of a series of Rava's rulings on gentiles left alone with Jewish wine; in each, the wine stays permitted if the gentile would fear being watched.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled the wine permitted.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. Here the concern is that a gentile might pour out or dedicate wine as an offering to an idol, which would make it forbidden to Jews.

avodah_zarah-70a-3-3.note: A gentile was found sitting among the barrels at an inn where a Jew's wine was stored. Rava ruled that if he was caught like a thief, startled and without an excuse, the wine is permitted; if not, it is forbidden.
avodah_zarah-70a-3-3.why: It is one of a series of Rava's rulings on gentiles found alone with Jewish wine. Here a gentile who fears being caught is assumed not to have touched the wine.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the wine.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. Here the concern is that a gentile might pour out or dedicate wine as an offering to an idol, which would make it forbidden to Jews.

avodah_zarah-70a-4-4.note: A gentile was found standing among the barrels in a house where wine was stored. Rava ruled that if he had an excuse for being there, the wine is forbidden, and if not, it is permitted.
avodah_zarah-70a-4-4.why: It continues Rava's rulings on gentiles found with Jewish wine. The Gemara challenges it from a teaching that wine in a locked inn is forbidden, and answers that the teaching means a gentile who had an excuse for being there.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the wine.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. Here the concern is that a gentile might pour out or dedicate wine as an offering to an idol, which would make it forbidden to Jews.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

avodah_zarah-70a-5-5.note: A Jew and a gentile were sitting and drinking wine together when the Jew heard the sound of prayer from the synagogue, got up and went. Rava ruled the wine permitted, since the gentile would think the Jew might remember his wine at any moment and come back.
avodah_zarah-70a-5-5.why: It is one of a series of Rava's rulings on gentiles left alone with Jewish wine: if the gentile expects the Jew back at any moment, the wine stays permitted.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled the wine permitted.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. Here the concern is that a gentile might pour out or dedicate wine as an offering to an idol, which would make it forbidden to Jews.

avodah_zarah-70a-6-6.note: A Jew and a gentile were sitting on a ship when the Jew heard the shofar blown at twilight before Shabbat, got off and went into town. Rava ruled the wine permitted, since the gentile would think the Jew might remember his wine at any moment and come back.
avodah_zarah-70a-6-6.why: It is one of Rava's rulings on gentiles left alone with Jewish wine. The Gemara then defends it: one might think the gentile knows the Jew will not return on Shabbat, but Issur the Convert said gentiles assume Jews break Shabbat for money.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled the wine permitted.

terms.meaning: A ram's horn blown toward evening on Friday to announce that Shabbat, the day of rest, is about to begin.

avodah_zarah-70a-8-8.note: A lion roared in a winepress, and a gentile who heard it was frightened and hid among the barrels of wine. Rava ruled the wine permitted, since the gentile would think that just as he was hiding, a Jew might also be hiding behind him and watching.
avodah_zarah-70a-8-8.why: It is one of a series of Rava's rulings on gentiles alone with Jewish wine, where the wine stays permitted if the gentile would fear being seen.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled the wine permitted.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. Here the concern is that a gentile might pour out or dedicate wine as an offering to an idol, which would make it forbidden to Jews.

avodah_zarah-70a-9-9.note: Thieves came to Pumbedita and opened many barrels of wine. Rava ruled the wine permitted, because most thieves there are Jews. A similar incident happened in Nehardea, and Shmuel also ruled the wine permitted.
avodah_zarah-70a-9-9.why: The Gemara asks whether this follows Rabbi Eliezer's view on doubt about entering a place, then answers that it is a double doubt: the thieves may have been Jews, and gentile thieves might have opened the barrels looking for money.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled the Pumbedita wine permitted.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who ruled the same way in a similar case in Nehardea.

avodah_zarah-72b-8-8.note: A man was siphoning wine out of a barrel through a large tube and a small tube when a gentile came and rested his hand on the large tube. Rava declared all of the wine forbidden, including what was still in the barrel.
avodah_zarah-72b-8-8.why: The Gemara has been asking whether a stream of poured liquid connects the wine at both ends. Rava's students ask if this ruling proves it; Rava says no, since all the wine in the barrel was being drawn toward the tubes.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who declared the wine forbidden.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. Here the concern is that a gentile might pour out or dedicate wine as an offering to an idol, which would make it forbidden to Jews.

avodah_zarah-74b-3-3.note: A man asked Rabbi Hiyya for someone to purify a winepress he had bought from a gentile. Rabbi Hiyya sent Rav, telling him not to give people cause to complain about him in the study hall. Rav saw the press was smooth with pitch and decided cleansing would be enough. But walking around it, he spotted a crack full of wine underneath, and concluded the pitch must be peeled off. That, he said, was what his uncle meant by his warning.
avodah_zarah-74b-3-3.why: It illustrates Rava's view that a winepress the gentile used to tread grapes needs more than cleansing; cleansing is enough only if he merely lined it with pitch.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage the man asked for help; Rav calls him his uncle.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's nephew, sent to purify the winepress.

terms.meaning: A tar-like coating used to seal winepresses and jars. It can absorb wine, so the question is how to clean it.
The house of study where the Sages met and debated; Rabbi Hiyya feared criticism there.
Rav's affectionate word for Rabbi Hiyya, translated here as 'my uncle'.

avodah_zarah-76a-17-17.note: A large cauldron in the house of Rav Akavya needed to be purged. He put a rim of dough around its mouth, filled it with water and boiled it, so the water boiled up to its edge. Rava said only a great man like Rav Akavya would be clever enough to do this: just as the rim absorbs forbidden food in small drops, it gives it out in small drops of boiling water.
avodah_zarah-76a-17-17.why: Rav Huna had said a small kettle is purged by dipping it into a large kettle of boiling water. The Gemara asks what to do with a large kettle, and this incident is the answer.

people.name: Rav Akavya
people.about: The man whose cauldron was purged; Rava calls him a great man.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who praised and explained Rav Akavya's method.

terms.meaning: To clean a cooking vessel of forbidden food it has absorbed, by boiling water in it or immersing it in boiling water.

avodah_zarah-76b-2-3.note: Mar Yehuda and Bati bar Tuvi, a wealthy man, were sitting before Shapur, the king of Persia, when an etrog was brought in. The king cut a slice and ate it, cut a slice for Bati bar Tuvi, then stuck the knife into the ground ten times before cutting a slice for Mar Yehuda. Bati bar Tuvi protested that he too was Jewish; the king answered that he was certain Mar Yehuda was careful about Jewish law but not certain about him. Another version has the king say: remember what you did last night.
avodah_zarah-76b-2-3.why: The Gemara has just taught that a good knife thrust ten times into hard ground is clean enough for cutting cold food; the king's treatment of the knife shows that very practice.

people.name: Mar Yehuda
people.about: An important figure of the Exilarch's house, whom the king trusts to keep Jewish law.

people.name: Bati bar Tuvi
people.about: A wealthy Jewish man sitting with Mar Yehuda before the king.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: The king of Persia, who hosts the two men and cuts the etrog.

terms.meaning: A citron, a fragrant citrus fruit.
Jewish law.

avodah_zarah-18a-3-3.note: Rabbi Yohanan tells that the daughter of Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon was once walking before the nobles of Rome, who remarked on how pleasant her steps were. At once she took care to keep walking so that her steps would go on pleasing them. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish links this to the verse "The iniquity of my heel encircles me": the small sins a person tramples underfoot in this world surround him on the Day of Judgment.
avodah_zarah-18a-3-3.why: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon's daughter was sentenced to sit in a brothel; the Gemara, having explained why he and his wife were punished, asks why she was, and this incident is the answer.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who tells the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon
people.about: Her father, a Sage condemned by the Romans.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: A Sage whose reading of a verse in Psalms the Gemara links to the incident.

terms.meaning: The time when God judges each person's deeds.

avodah_zarah-39a-10-10.note: Rabba bar bar Hana had been served a dish of small fish and heard a man call it by the name of a non-kosher sea creature. He reasoned that the name meant something non-kosher was in it, and he did not eat it that night. In the morning he examined the dish and found something non-kosher in it. He applied to himself the verse "No sin shall befall the righteous."
avodah_zarah-39a-10-10.why: The Gemara is collecting incidents of Sages judging doubtful fish; this one ends with a Sage saved from eating forbidden food by a chance remark.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Sage who refused a fish dish after hearing it given a non-kosher name, and was proven right.
